title: Amba's choice
hookLine: Bhishma carries off three princesses, the eldest says she has already chosen, and why brides still hold the garland
carry: the bride's garland is her choice
tomorrow: The vow that would not bend

cards: Word reaches Hastinapura: the king of Kashi's three daughters will choose their husbands at a swayamvara, a self-choice, with kings gathered from everywhere.
Vichitravirya is now a young man, and Bhishma has decided he should marry. So, with Satyavati's leave, Bhishma rides alone to Varanasi. He isn't going there to be chosen.

teach.b: The kings laugh at the old man come courting. He answers by lifting the three princesses onto his chariot. He names the ways a bride may be won, and says the wise think well of a bride taken by force.
The kings take up weapons, and he defeats them all, among them Shalva, king of Saubha. Then he brings the sisters home to Satyavati, as if they were his daughters, the text says.
It's a hard scene to hear today, and the text tells it plainly. Then the story turns.
As the wedding is prepared, the eldest, Amba, speaks.
In my heart, she tells Bhishma, I had already chosen Shalva, and he had chosen me. You know dharma. Do what's right.
And the man who just won her by force stops. He asks the learned men of the court, and lets her go to Shalva. Her story isn't over; the poem comes back to her much later.
The younger two marry Vichitravirya, who some years later falls ill and dies young, with no son. Now the teaching.
The swayamvara was the epics' way of honoring a bride's choosing: Damayanti chose Nala at hers, and Draupadi's comes later in this poem.
Amba's choice was already made, and when she named it as dharma, even the strongest man in the kingdom gave way. Hindu weddings still keep a trace of this.
In the jaimala, or varmala, bride and groom place garlands on each other, and many families say it remembers the swayamvara, when a princess garlanded the one she chose.

how: In many Hindu weddings the couple exchange garlands, the jaimala or varmala, and many families say it recalls the swayamvara, where a princess placed a garland on the man she chose.

Bhishma let Amba go after she spoke
he consulted the learned men and sent her to Shalva.

games.q: at a Hindu wedding, your friend asks why the bride puts a garland on the groom. what fits?
o: many families say it remembers the swayamvara: the bride choosing too.
it shows the groom's family paid for the wedding.
it's only there to look nice in photos.
games.why: in the epics a princess garlanded the one she chose. Amba's choice, named as dharma, made even Bhishma let her go.

practice: Before a big step, many Hindus stop at the home shrine and set their intention before God. Bring to mind one choice that's truly yours to make, small or large. Hold it the way Amba held hers: clearly.
If you pray, place it before God in your own words; if not, say it once to yourself, plainly. Notice how naming it steadies you.

wordCard.voice: Satyavati. A queen mother whose house gains two brides, lets one go free, and loses its young king.

orig.note: Sanskrit svayamvara: the self-choice, where a princess picks her husband from gathered suitors.

carryVoice: Your line: the bride's garland is her choice. Amba named hers, and a hard story turned. That's day seven hundred nineteen.
